questions.question:
D1 — Empathy narrative: does this match the EvalKit getting-started reality?

Here's what I traced from README.md and the docs. The persona: Python ML engineer who just heard about EvalKit and wants to verify it works locally before integrating it into their team's CI pipeline.

> T+0:00 — I open the README. "Install with python -m pip install evalkit==2.0.0b1, set EVALKIT_API_KEY, then follow the quickstart's command: python examples/first_eval.py." Three steps. Looks easy.
>
> T+1:00 — pip install succeeds. I set the key. I run the README's quickstart command: python examples/first_eval.py. I get an error. The file doesn't exist — it's not in the installed package and there's no examples/ directory anywhere.
>
> T+2:00 — I dig into the README more carefully and find python -m evalkit.demo mentioned as an alternative. I try that.
>
> T+2:30 — The demo starts. It prints: "Waiting for CI check: 0s elapsed of 300s". 300 seconds. Five minutes. I'm on my laptop doing a local trial. No one told me a remote CI check was part of the deal.
>
> T+7:30 — The CI check finishes. I see the demo scores. The output looks good. But I've just spent seven and a half minutes on a "quick start" that started with a missing-file error and a five-minute surprise wait.

Does this match reality? Where am I wrong? <gstack-qid:devex-review-empathy-narrative>

options.label: Accurate — proceed
options.description: The narrative is correct. Proceed with this understanding for the full DX review. (recommended)

options.label: Partly wrong — let me correct it
options.description: Some details are off; I'll clarify before we continue.

options.label: Wrong path — the actual flow is different
options.description: The real getting-started path differs significantly from what was traced.

questions.question:
D2 — Journey stage INSTALL: the quickstart file in the README doesn't exist in the package

README.md says: "follow the quickstart's command: python examples/first_eval.py". docs/package-contents.txt confirms that `examples/first_eval.py` is absent from both the published package and the release examples archive. The Python ML engineer hits a file-not-found error as their very first action after install.

This violates DX First Principle #1 (Zero friction at T0): the README-documented command fails immediately.

Stakes if we skip: every developer who follows the README's own quickstart instruction hits an error before they ever see a real evaluation result. This is the definition of a broken first impression.

Recommendation: A — update the README to use `python -m evalkit.demo` as the primary quickstart command, because the demo module is the one that actually works and ships with the package.

Completeness: A=9/10, B=6/10, C=5/10

Pros / cons:

A) Update README to use `python -m evalkit.demo` (recommended)
  ✅ Removes the broken command from the documented happy path; works out of the box
  ✅ Aligns README with the terminal demo delivery vehicle that was already chosen
  ❌ Loses the examples/first_eval.py pattern if some users prefer a file they can edit

B) Add examples/first_eval.py to the published package
  ✅ Preserves the quickstart file as an editable starting point for users
  ❌ Requires building and shipping the file; doesn't fix the TTHW problem independently

C) Keep both paths, note in README that the examples archive is optional
  ✅ Gives users two entry points
  ❌ Two paths creates "choose your own adventure" confusion at the worst possible moment

Net: A is a one-line README fix that removes a broken command. B and C require more work and don't deliver a cleaner first experience. <gstack-qid:devex-review-missing-quickstart-file>

options.label: A — Update README to use python -m evalkit.demo (recommended)
options.description: Remove the broken examples/first_eval.py command from the README; make python -m evalkit.demo the documented quickstart.

options.label: B — Add examples/first_eval.py to the package
options.description: Ship the quickstart file so the README command works.

options.label: C — Keep both, add a note
options.description: Document that examples archive is optional and python -m evalkit.demo is the fallback.

answers.D2 — Journey stage INSTALL: the quicksta: A — Update README to use python -m evalkit.demo (recommended)

questions.question:
D3 — Journey stage HELLO WORLD: the mandatory 5-minute CI gate makes the <2-minute TTHW target unreachable

docs/benchmarks.md sets the agreed target at under 2 minutes. docs/current-contracts.md says the beta plan retains a mandatory 5-minute remote CI wait on every developer's first local evaluation, with no skip flag and no offline path. Those two things cannot both be true.

With the CI gate: pip install (~60s) + set key (~10s) + run demo + 300s wait = ~6 minutes. This is where the benchmark's 6-minute measurement came from.
Without the CI gate: pip install + set key + run demo + see scores = roughly 90 seconds. Under 2 minutes. Target achieved.

This violates DX First Principle #1 (Zero friction at T0) and the Incremental Steps principle: the developer cannot get ANY local result before a 5-minute mandatory remote round-trip. The empathy narrative shows they don't expect this and aren't warned before it starts.

Stakes if we skip: the plan ships with a stated TTHW target it is architecturally incapable of hitting. The benchmark study becomes misleading. The Python ML engineer who wanted a local result before CI finds that even the local demo requires CI.

Recommendation: A — add a skip flag (e.g., EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK=1 or --skip-ci-check) for local/demo runs, because this preserves the production safety gate for real CI while enabling the <2-minute demo path.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Pros / cons:

A) Add a local-run skip flag (EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK or --no-ci-check) (recommended)
  ✅ Unlocks the <2-minute demo path; the production CI gate still runs in real pipelines
  ✅ Aligns with DX principle #4 (Decide for me, let me override): gate ON by default in prod, OFF for local trial
  ❌ Requires documenting the flag clearly so developers know when to use it safely

B) Retain gate, update TTHW target to be 6 minutes and document the CI wait upfront
  ✅ No code change; the existing behavior is fully documented
  ❌ Abandons the agreed under-2-minute target; places EvalKit in the "Needs Work" TTHW tier with measurably lower adoption

C) Keep gate, add a progress bar and estimated time to the wait message
  ✅ Developer knows what is happening and how long it will take; reduces abandonment from surprise
  ❌ Does not change the TTHW — the wait is still 5 minutes; TTHW target still unreachable

Net: A is the only option that makes both the target AND the production gate achievable. B and C accept a broken TTHW target. <gstack-qid:devex-review-ci-gate-tthw>

options.label: A — Add a local skip flag for demo/local runs (recommended)
options.description: Add EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK=1 or --no-ci-check so the <2-minute target is reachable while the production gate is preserved.

options.label: B — Retain gate, update the TTHW target to 6 minutes
options.description: Accept the 5-minute gate as a hard requirement and document it prominently; drop the under-2-minute target.

options.label: C — Retain gate, improve the wait UX with better messaging
options.description: Add a progress bar and explicit estimated time to the CI wait output; TTHW target is still unachievable.

answers.D3 — Journey stage HELLO WORLD: the mand: A — Add a local skip flag for demo/local runs (recommended)

questions.question:
D4 — Pass 3 (Error Messages): AuthError("request failed") is a dead end

docs/api.md documents: "For an invalid API key, the SDK raises AuthError('request failed'). There is no authentication error code, explanation of the cause, or instruction for replacing the key. The plan retains this message."

What the Python ML engineer sees when they set the wrong key or forget to export it:
  AuthError: request failed

What they need:
  AuthError: Authentication failed — your EVALKIT_API_KEY is invalid or expired.
  Set a valid key: export EVALKIT_API_KEY=<your-key>
  Get your key at: https://evalkit.example.com/dashboard/api-keys

The Hall of Fame formula: problem + cause + fix + where to learn more. The current message scores 1/4: it names the error class but omits cause, fix, and docs link. A developer hitting this for the first time will search their shell, re-read the README, and wonder if the SDK is broken.

This violates DX First Principle #5 (Fight uncertainty): every error must identify problem, cause, and fix. Auth errors are the most common first-run failure for any API SDK.

Stakes if we skip: developers who mistype their key or use a test key abandon the SDK in minute 3 with no path forward. Support tickets spike on "why does it say request failed?"

Recommendation: A — update the error message to include cause + fix + link, because the cost is one string change and the impact is turning a dead end into a resolved issue.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Pros / cons:

A) Update AuthError message: cause + fix instruction + API key URL (recommended)
  ✅ Developer knows exactly what went wrong and what to do next; no support ticket needed
  ✅ One-line change to the SDK; consistent with how all other errors already work per current-contracts.md
  ❌ Requires publishing a new SDK version if the message is in compiled code

B) Retain current message, add a troubleshooting section to the docs
  ✅ No SDK code change required
  ❌ Developer must leave the terminal, find the docs, and navigate to troubleshooting — context-switch cost of 10-20 minutes

Net: A costs one string edit. B costs the developer 10 minutes of confusion every time. <gstack-qid:devex-review-auth-error-message>

options.label: A — Fix the error message: cause + fix + link (recommended)
options.description: Update AuthError to include what failed, why, and how to fix it (set a valid key, link to dashboard).

options.label: B — Keep message, add troubleshooting docs
options.description: Document the auth error in a separate troubleshooting page; don't change the SDK error text.

answers.D4 — Pass 3 (Error Messages): AuthError(: A — Fix the error message: cause + fix + link (recommended)

questions.question:
D5 — Pass 2 (API Design): run_eval and run_batch take the same arguments in reversed order

docs/api.md documents:
  run_eval(dataset, evaluator)
  run_batch(evaluator, dataset)

Both argument names describe the same concepts. The reversed positional order is documented as "intentional" and neither function requires keyword arguments.

A Python ML engineer who learns run_eval(dataset, evaluator) and then picks up run_batch will silently pass the arguments in the wrong order. There is no TypeError — both arguments are valid Python objects. The call succeeds, the results are wrong, and the developer spends 30 minutes debugging why their batch evaluations are nonsense.

This violates DX First Principle #4 (Decide for me) and the Hall of Fame anti-pattern "God endpoint / inconsistent naming": identical concepts should follow identical calling conventions. The Stripe API is the gold standard for consistency — you never have to wonder if it's customer, charge or charge, customer.

Stakes if we skip: silent bugs in production. Developers who use both functions will be bitten exactly once, file a confusing bug report, and lose trust in the SDK.

Recommendation: A — standardize to (dataset, evaluator) order in both functions, because dataset is the primary noun in evaluation and should always come first.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Pros / cons:

A) Standardize to run_eval(dataset, evaluator) / run_batch(dataset, evaluator) (recommended)
  ✅ Consistent calling convention; developers who learn one API use the other correctly by muscle memory
  ✅ Eliminates the silent-wrong-order bug before it hits any user
  ❌ Breaking change to run_batch — requires changelog entry and migration note

B) Require keyword arguments on both functions
  ✅ Positional ambiguity is gone; callers must name their args
  ❌ Adding keyword-only enforcement is also a breaking change; heavier than swapping order

C) Keep current order, add a type annotation or runtime check that warns on likely-wrong-order calls
  ✅ No API change
  ❌ Heuristic check is fragile; if both args are the same type, it can't detect the swap

Net: A is a surgical fix that costs one v2 changelog line. The alternative is leaving a silent bug that will confuse every developer who uses both functions. <gstack-qid:devex-review-api-arg-order>

options.label: A — Standardize both functions to (dataset, evaluator) (recommended)
options.description: Align run_batch to match run_eval's argument order; add a migration note to the changelog.

options.label: B — Require keyword arguments on both functions
options.description: Make both functions keyword-only so callers must explicitly name dataset= and evaluator=.

options.label: C — Keep current order, add a runtime order-check hint
options.description: Leave the order as-is; add a best-effort runtime warning if arguments appear to be swapped.

answers.D5 — Pass 2 (API Design): run_eval and r: A — Standardize both functions to (dataset, evaluator) (recommended)

questions.question:
D6 — Pass 5 (Upgrade Path): v1→v2 removes Client.evaluate() with no warning, no guide, no codemod

docs/api.md documents: "Version 1 exposes Client.evaluate(). Version 2 replaces it with Client.run() and removes the old name immediately. No compatibility alias, deprecation warning, migration guide, or codemod is provided."

The Python ML engineer who is already using EvalKit v1 in their team's pipeline runs pip install --upgrade evalkit and gets:
  AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute 'evaluate'

No warning before the upgrade. No changelog entry pointing to the rename. No migration guide. Their production pipeline breaks. They have to grep their entire codebase for .evaluate( and manually replace each call with .run( — while a broken CI job waits.

This violates DX First Principle #7 (Speed is a feature) and DX Characteristic #2 (Credible): developers need to trust that upgrades won't silently break their work. TypeScript's gold standard is "never breaks JS" — or if it must break, a codemod does the migration automatically.

Stakes if we skip: every v1 user has their pipeline broken on upgrade with no recovery path except reading the source code. This is the kind of experience that causes teams to pin SDK versions forever and never upgrade again.

Recommendation: A — add a compatibility alias with a DeprecationWarning and a migration note in the changelog, because it costs one alias and one warning line and prevents every v1 user from hitting a production crash.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Pros / cons:

A) Add Client.evaluate() as a DeprecationWarning alias + changelog migration note (recommended)
  ✅ v1 code continues to work with a clear console warning; upgrade is non-breaking
  ✅ Changelog note + warning together tell the developer exactly what to change and where
  ❌ Old name stays in the codebase until the next major version; minor code debt

B) Add a migration guide to docs with find-replace instructions
  ✅ No SDK code change
  ❌ Developers must find the guide AFTER their pipeline breaks; no warning before or during the failure

C) Keep hard break, add an informative error message when evaluate() is called
  ✅ Developer gets an error that names the replacement method instead of "has no attribute"
  ❌ Still a breaking change that crashes the pipeline; just slightly less confusing

Net: A keeps every v1 user unbroken while they migrate. B and C still break production pipelines on upgrade. <gstack-qid:devex-review-v1-v2-migration>

options.label: A — Compatibility alias + DeprecationWarning + changelog note (recommended)
options.description: Keep Client.evaluate() working with a deprecation warning that names Client.run() as the replacement.

options.label: B — Keep hard break, add a migration guide to docs
options.description: Document the rename in a migration guide; accept that v1 code breaks on upgrade.

options.label: C — Keep hard break, add an informative AttributeError message
options.description: Raise a helpful error naming Client.run() when Client.evaluate() is called on v2.

answers.D6 — Pass 5 (Upgrade Path): v1→v2 remove: A — Compatibility alias + DeprecationWarning + changelog note (recommended)

The DX review found and resolved five P1 issues. All decisions were made (D2–D6). The implementation tasks (T1–T5) are waiting. The plan also needs an Eng Review before shipping.

What would you like to do next? <gstack-qid:devex-review-next-steps>

reportContent:
# DX Plan Review: EvalKit SDK 2.0.0b1 Beta Release Polish

## Context

EvalKit is a Python SDK for ML engineers evaluating LLM responses. This review was
requested to apply DX POLISH to the beta release — improving every developer-facing
touchpoint within the existing release scope. The plan identified five specific contracts
to review: the first-run CI requirement, public function signatures, authentication error,
packaged quickstart, and v1-to-v2 client upgrade. Four of the five had material DX gaps;
all were resolved through interactive review.

---

## Pre-Settled Decisions (from README.md + docs/benchmarks.md)

These were confirmed before the review began and are not re-litigated here.

- **Persona:** Python ML engineer. Uses terminal. Wants a local result before connecting to CI.
- **Mode:** DX POLISH — improve existing touchpoints within beta release scope; no expansion.
- **TTHW target:** under 2 minutes (established benchmark study target).
- **Competitive benchmark:** peers at 2–4 min; EvalKit currently at 6 min. Target: Champion tier.
- **Magical moment delivery:** copy-paste terminal command — `python -m evalkit.demo`.

---

## TARGET DEVELOPER PERSONA

```
Who:       Python ML engineer evaluating LLM responses
Context:   Wants to verify the SDK locally before integrating into their team's CI pipeline
Tolerance: 5–10 minutes max before abandoning; expects pip-native tooling, no surprises
Expects:   pip install, export key, run command, see scores — no Docker, no remote calls
```

---

## Developer Empathy Narrative

*First-person trace of the actual documented getting-started path — confirmed accurate by user.*

> T+0:00 — I open README.md. First heading: "EvalKit SDK." Description: Python SDK for ML
> engineers. This looks like me. I find "Getting started": three steps — install, set key,
> run quickstart. Looks fast.
>
> T+1:00 — `pip install evalkit==2.0.0b1` succeeds. I set EVALKIT_API_KEY in my shell. I run
> the README's quickstart: `python examples/first_eval.py`. I get an error: the file doesn't
> exist. It's not in the installed package. No examples/ directory anywhere.
>
> T+2:00 — I re-read the README more carefully and find `python -m evalkit.demo` mentioned as
> the demo. I try that instead.
>
> T+2:30 — The demo starts. It prints: "Waiting for CI check: 0s elapsed of 300s". 300 seconds.
> Five minutes. I'm on my laptop trying a local trial. I wasn't warned a remote CI check was
> part of the deal.
>
> T+7:30 — The CI check passes. I see demo scores. The output format is exactly right. But seven
> and a half minutes, one file-not-found error, and a surprise five-minute wall to get here.

---

## Competitive DX Benchmark

```
COMPETITIVE DX BENCHMARK
=========================
Tool       | TTHW     | Notable DX Choice               | Source
Peer SDK A | 2 min    | Clean local first run           | docs/benchmarks.md
Peer SDK B | 4 min    | —                               | docs/benchmarks.md
Peer SDK C | 3 min    | —                               | docs/benchmarks.md
EvalKit    | 6 min    | 5-min mandatory CI gate         | docs/benchmarks.md (measured)
EvalKit*   | ~90 sec  | With EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK      | post-review target
```

Target tier: **Champion (< 2 minutes)** — achievable with the skip flag added in D3.

---

## Magical Moment Specification

**Chosen delivery vehicle:** Copy-paste terminal command — `python -m evalkit.demo`

The demo evaluates bundled sample responses and prints real per-example scores plus an
aggregate score. No hosted playground needed. No install beyond the package itself.
Expected output:

```
example 1: score=0.80
example 2: score=1.00
overall: score=0.90
```

**Requirement from this review:** The demo must be reachable in under 2 minutes. This
requires the EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK flag (D3) to exist and be documented in the README.

---

## Developer Journey Map (post-review)

```
STAGE           | DEVELOPER DOES                         | FRICTION POINTS            | STATUS
----------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------|--------
1. Discover     | Opens README; reads description        | None                       | OK
2. Install      | pip install evalkit==2.0.0b1           | None (one command)         | OK
3. Hello World  | export EVALKIT_API_KEY + run demo      | Quickstart file missing;   | FIXED (D2, D3)
                |                                        | CI gate blocks TTHW target |
4. Real Usage   | run_eval / run_batch in own pipeline   | Reversed arg order silent  | FIXED (D5)
                |                                        | bug between the two funcs  |
5. Debug        | Invalid API key path                   | AuthError("request failed")| FIXED (D4)
                |                                        | gives no cause or fix      |
6. Upgrade      | pip install --upgrade evalkit          | v1 Client.evaluate() crash | FIXED (D6)
                |                                        | with no warning or guide   |
```

---

## First-Time Developer Confusion Report

```
FIRST-TIME DEVELOPER REPORT
============================
Persona:    Python ML engineer; pip-native; no Docker; wants local result first
Attempting: EvalKit getting started

CONFUSION LOG:
T+1:00  Runs README quickstart: python examples/first_eval.py → FileNotFoundError.
        Nothing in the README explains this. Digs back through README for an alternative.
T+2:30  Finds python -m evalkit.demo. Runs it. Sees "Waiting for CI check: 300s."
        Was not expecting remote round-trip for a local demo. Considers Ctrl-C.
T+7:30  Succeeds. Output is clear and useful. Trust partially restored.

ITEMS ADDRESSED:
✅ #1 Missing file → README updated to use python -m evalkit.demo (D2)
✅ #2 CI gate surprise → EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK flag added; README documents it (D3)
```

---

## DX Findings & Decisions

### D2 — Missing quickstart file (P1 — blocks T0)

**Finding:** README.md documents `python examples/first_eval.py` as the quickstart. That
file is absent from the published package and the release examples archive (confirmed in
`docs/package-contents.txt`). Every developer who follows the README's own instructions
hits a FileNotFoundError as their first action after install.

**Decision: A** — Update README to use `python -m evalkit.demo` as the primary quickstart
command. The demo module ships with the package and produces the expected output.

**Plan change:** README.md quickstart section — replace `python examples/first_eval.py`
with `python -m evalkit.demo`.

---

### D3 — CI gate makes <2-minute TTHW impossible (P1 — blocks TTHW target)

**Finding:** `docs/current-contracts.md` documents a mandatory 5-minute remote CI check on
every developer's first local evaluation. No skip flag. No offline path. The plan retains
this gate. `docs/benchmarks.md` sets the agreed TTHW target at under 2 minutes. With the
CI gate: ~6 minutes. Without it: ~90 seconds. These two requirements cannot coexist without
an escape hatch.

**Decision: A** — Add a local-run skip flag so developers can reach the demo in under 2
minutes while the production CI gate remains active for real pipelines.

**Plan change:** Add `EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK=1` environment variable (and optionally
`--no-ci-check` CLI flag) to bypass the first-run CI gate. Document in README alongside the
demo command. Production usage: gate remains on by default. Local/demo usage: flag explicitly
disables it.

---

### D4 — AuthError("request failed") is a dead end (P1 — breaks first-run for wrong-key users)

**Finding:** `docs/api.md`: "For an invalid API key, the SDK raises `AuthError('request
failed')`. There is no authentication error code, explanation of the cause, or instruction
for replacing the key." Auth errors are the most common first-run failure for any API SDK.
The current message scores 1/4 on the Hall of Fame formula (problem only; no cause, no fix,
no docs link).

**Decision: A** — Update the error message to include cause, fix instruction, and docs link.

**Plan change:** `evalkit/client.py` auth error path — update message to:
```
AuthError: Authentication failed — your EVALKIT_API_KEY is invalid or expired.
Set a valid key: export EVALKIT_API_KEY=<your-key>
Get your key at: https://evalkit.example.com/dashboard/api-keys
```

---

### D5 — run_eval / run_batch have reversed argument order (P1 — silent bug)

**Finding:** `docs/api.md` documents `run_eval(dataset, evaluator)` and
`run_batch(evaluator, dataset)`. Same argument names, reversed positional order, no
keyword-argument requirement. A developer who learns one function and then uses the other
passes arguments in the wrong order. No TypeError — both are valid Python objects. Results
are silently wrong. 30-minute debugging sessions follow.

**Decision: A** — Standardize both functions to `(dataset, evaluator)`. Dataset is the
primary noun; it should always come first.

**Plan change:** `evalkit/client.py` or equivalent — swap `run_batch`'s argument order to
`run_batch(dataset, evaluator)`. Add changelog entry noting the signature alignment.

---

### D6 — v1→v2 removes Client.evaluate() with no warning or migration path (P1 — breaks v1 users)

**Finding:** `docs/api.md`: "Version 1 exposes `Client.evaluate()`. Version 2 replaces it
with `Client.run()` and removes the old name immediately. No compatibility alias,
deprecation warning, migration guide, or codemod is provided." Every v1 user running
`pip install --upgrade evalkit` gets an immediate `AttributeError` with no recovery path
except reading source code.

**Decision: A** — Add `Client.evaluate()` as a `DeprecationWarning` alias pointing to
`Client.run()`, plus a migration note in the changelog.

**Plan change:**
- `evalkit/client.py` — add: `def evaluate(self, *args, **kwargs): warnings.warn("Client.evaluate() is deprecated; use Client.run() instead", DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2); return self.run(*args, **kwargs)`
- Changelog — add migration note: "`Client.evaluate()` renamed to `Client.run()`; old name raises DeprecationWarning and will be removed in v3."

---

## NOT In Scope

The following DX improvements were considered and explicitly deferred per the "DX POLISH,
existing release scope" mandate in the plan.

- **Interactive playground / sandbox** — no new hosted service in this release (current-contracts.md)
- **Additional language bindings** — Python only; no new bindings proposed (current-contracts.md)
- **Community program / channels** — no new community program proposed (current-contracts.md)
- **Codemod for run_batch argument flip** — manual migration is sufficient for beta; codemod appropriate for GA

---

## What Already Exists (reuse baseline)

Per `docs/current-contracts.md`, the following are working and should not be changed:

- Type annotations, offline sample data, mock transport — all exist and work
- Noninteractive CI mode — exists
- API reference, support contact, changelog, contributor guide — all exist
- Telemetry is opt-in
- All non-AuthError errors already include: cause, relevant argument/file, actionable fix, secret redaction
- API timeouts, cancellation, rate limits, retries bounded and documented
- Evaluation IDs prevent duplicate submitted jobs
- Python 3.10+, macOS, Linux, Windows without Docker — all supported
- Timing instrumentation and post-beta feedback survey — both exist

---

## DX Scorecard

```
+====================================================================+
|              DX PLAN REVIEW — SCORECARD                            |
+====================================================================+
| Dimension            | Score  | Prior  | Trend  |
|----------------------|--------|--------|--------|
| Getting Started      |  8/10  |  2/10  |  +6 ↑  |
| API/CLI/SDK          |  8/10  |  4/10  |  +4 ↑  |
| Error Messages       |  8/10  |  4/10  |  +4 ↑  |
| Documentation        |  7/10  |  5/10  |  +2 ↑  |
| Upgrade Path         |  8/10  |  1/10  |  +7 ↑  |
| Dev Environment      |  8/10  |  8/10  |   0 →  |
| Community            |  6/10  |  6/10  |   0 →  |
| DX Measurement       |  8/10  |  8/10  |   0 →  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| TTHW                 | ~90sec |  6min  |  -4.5m ↑|
| Competitive Rank     | Champion (< 2 min, post-fix)                |
| Magical Moment       | designed via copy-paste terminal command     |
```
